genZNote: Glows yellow-green under a Wood's lamp — the one dermatophyte exam question that actually has a visual answer.

morphology.shape: Septate hyphae with large, spindle-shaped, thick-walled macroconidia

habitat.naturalHabitat: Skin, fur, and claws of cats and dogs (zoophilic dermatophyte)
habitat.hostAssociation: Zoonotic — cats (especially kittens) are the primary reservoir; transmitted to humans via direct animal contact
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Can persist on fomites (bedding, grooming tools) contaminated with infected hair/skin

microscopy.stain: KOH wet mount of skin/hair; lactophenol cotton blue of culture
microscopy.appearance: Septate hyphae; large spindle-shaped macroconidia with rough, echinulate (spiny) walls on culture

culture.media: Sabouraud dextrose agar, dermatophyte test medium (DTM)
culture.growthCharacteristics: Obligate aerobe; grows over 1-2 weeks at room temperature; turns DTM red due to alkaline metabolites
culture.pigmentation: Yellow-orange reverse pigmentation on Sabouraud agar

biochemicalTests.test: Wood's lamp examination of infected hair

identificationClues: Infected hair fluoresces bright yellow-green under a Wood's lamp — a classic bedside diagnostic clue
Large, spindle-shaped, rough-walled (echinulate) macroconidia on culture, distinguishing it from Trichophyton species
History of contact with a cat or dog, especially a kitten
Common cause of tinea capitis in children

diseases: Tinea capitis (scalp ringworm), especially in children — can cause patchy hair loss with scaling and inflammation
Tinea corporis (body ringworm) — annular, scaly, erythematous plaques
virulenceFactors: Keratinase enzymes allowing invasion of keratinized tissue (hair, skin)
Ability to invade the hair shaft (ectothrix infection pattern)
clinicalImportance.transmission: Direct contact with an infected cat or dog, or indirectly via contaminated fomites (grooming tools, bedding)
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: One of the most common causes of tinea capitis in children, especially where household pet exposure is common; can cause outbreaks among family members and classmates
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Wood's lamp fluorescence of infected hairs is a fast, useful screening tool at the bedside, though a negative Wood's lamp does not exclude all dermatophyte infections since not every species fluoresces

examFacts.importantDisease: Tinea capitis in children, acquired from cats/dogs
examFacts.importantTest: Wood's lamp examination; KOH microscopy showing ectothrix hair invasion
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: A zoophilic dermatophyte from cats that fluoresces yellow-green under a Wood's lamp — unlike most Trichophyton species
